author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Compare Vulkan and OpenGL on one PS2 title
summary: Hold resolution, accuracy, driver, and scene fixed while measuring cold startup, warm frame pacing, graphics correctness, readbacks, and lifecycle stability on each API, then keep a per-game result backed by repeatable evidence.
heroAlt: Official PCSX2 Vulkan renderer artwork representing a controlled API comparison

blocks.text: Define one workload before selecting an API

Renderer choice should be based on the same title, device, driver, and scene. Choose an effects-heavy route containing ordinary gameplay, a framebuffer effect, and a transition or pause/resume event. Record the global settings, then copy them into two temporary per-game profiles that differ only by Vulkan or OpenGL.
Do not compare a cold shader-compiling Vulkan run against a warmed OpenGL run, or change internal resolution while switching APIs. That measures different workloads.

items: A saved route lasting at least two minutes with repeatable inputs.
Identical internal resolution, blending, mipmapping, filtering, aspect, and speed values.
The same system GPU driver for both APIs.
Cold-start and warm-session performance counters.
Screenshots of effects, HUD, and transition frames.

blocks.text: Run cold, warm, and lifecycle passes

items: 1. Restart the app, select Vulkan, cold-boot the route, and record initialization time plus any shader pauses.
2. Repeat the route warm and record median frame time, spikes, readbacks, uploads, and sustained speed.
3. Capture the predefined effect and transition frames.
4. Close the session, select OpenGL, and repeat the same cold and warm sequence.
5. Compare visual evidence before ranking performance; an API that omits effects does not win by being faster.
6. Background and resume the app once on each API, then reconnect an external display if that is normal use.
7. Repeat the apparent winner after the device is thermally warm.
8. Save the renderer only for this title and retain the losing profile for later driver regression checks.

blocks.text: Vulkan and OpenGL can expose different driver quality, synchronization cost, blending support, and cache behavior. Cold timing reveals initialization; warm timing represents play; screenshots catch correctness; lifecycle tests reveal swapchain or resume faults. A single peak FPS number cannot summarize those dimensions.
Choose the API that wins the complete repeatable workload.

items: Required graphics effects match the correctness reference.
Warm frame pacing stays stable through the full route.
Cold startup completes consistently after a reboot.
Pause, resume, rotation, and display reconnect do not lose the surface.
The selected API remains stable after thermal warm-up.
Settings indicators differ beyond the renderer: discard the pair and normalize profiles.
One run compiles shaders while the other uses cache: repeat matched cold or warm states.
A custom driver is used on only one API: restore the same system package.
Camera timing or game state changes: reload the in-game checkpoint and recapture both.

blocks.text: Restore the original global renderer, delete only the two comparison overrides, and cold-boot the title. Keep the evidence table and screenshots so a later emulator or driver update can repeat the same route.
Desktop guidance is a reference, not an Android guarantee

PCSX2 documents renderer behavior on its supported desktop platforms. EmuCoreX must still validate the Android device, driver, and lifecycle directly rather than assuming identical performance rankings.
